question: Under Texas Parks & Wildlife Code Section 31.095 (Excessive Speed), what standard governs how fast a boat may lawfully be operated?
choice_a: A single statewide maximum of 35 mph that applies on all public water regardless of conditions
choice_b: Any speed the operator personally judges to be safe, since Texas sets no speed standard for vessels
choice_c: A speed that is reasonable and prudent for the existing conditions and hazards, and that allows the operator to stop the boat within the assured clear distance ahead
choice_d: A speed limit fixed solely by the vessel's hull length, unrelated to conditions or traffic
explanation: Texas law prohibits operating a boat faster than is reasonable and prudent given conditions like weather and traffic density, or faster than allows the operator to stop within the assured clear distance ahead -- the same 'assured clear distance' concept used for vehicle speed laws.
source_note: Texas Water Safety Act / Parks & Wildlife Code Sec. 31.095 -- Excessive Speed

question: Besides staying out of posted no-wake zones, what does Texas Parks & Wildlife Code Section 31.098 separately require of motorboat operators?
choice_a: Nothing further -- wake regulation in Texas applies only inside marked no-wake zones
choice_b: A requirement that all wakes exceeding one foot in height be reported to TPWD
choice_c: A rule that applies only to vessels longer than 40 feet
choice_d: A general prohibition on operating a motorboat so as to create a hazardous wake or wash, which can apply even outside a marked no-wake zone
explanation: Texas law separately prohibits operating a motorboat in a way that creates a hazardous wake or wash, a general duty that is not limited to posted no-wake areas.
source_note: Parks & Wildlife Code Sec. 31.098 -- Hazardous Wake or Wash

question: Under Texas law, may a boat operator circle a vessel whose occupant is fishing or water skiing, or circle a swimmer?
choice_a: No -- operating a motorboat in a circular course around such a vessel, PWC, or swimmer is prohibited, except when circling to retrieve a downed or fallen water skier or similar person
choice_b: Yes, circling another vessel or a swimmer is always legal regardless of the circumstances
choice_c: It is legal only if the circling boat stays below 5 mph
choice_d: It is legal as long as the circling boat has no passengers aboard
explanation: Texas law prohibits operating a motorboat in a circular course around a vessel or PWC whose occupant is fishing, water skiing, or engaged in a similar activity, or around a swimmer, with a specific exception for retrieving a downed or fallen skier.
source_note: Parks & Wildlife Code Sec. 31.099 -- Prohibition on Circular Course Around Individuals Engaged in Water Activities

question: May a boater in Texas legally moor a boat to a navigational buoy, beacon, or marker, or move, damage, or otherwise tamper with it?
choice_a: Yes, any navigational marker placed on public water may be freely used for mooring
choice_b: No -- Texas law prohibits mooring or attaching a boat to a buoy, beacon, light marker, stake, flag, or other aid to safe operation, and separately prohibits moving, removing, displacing, damaging, or tampering with those aids
choice_c: Tampering with a marker is legal as long as it is done at night
choice_d: Only markers owned by a private marina may be used this way; state-placed markers may not
explanation: Texas law bars mooring or attaching a boat to a buoy, beacon, marker, stake, or flag placed by state or federal authority, and separately bars moving, removing, damaging, or tampering with such aids to safe operation.
source_note: Parks & Wildlife Code Sec. 31.100 -- Interference With Markers or Ramps

question: Under Texas law, when may a vessel legally be moored or attached to a state-owned boat launching ramp?
choice_a: At any time, for any purpose, including using the ramp as an overnight parking spot
choice_b: State ramps may never be used for mooring under any circumstance, even briefly
choice_c: Only in connection with launching or retrieving a boat from the water
choice_d: Only between the hours of sunset and sunrise
explanation: Texas law limits mooring or attaching a vessel to a state-owned boat launching ramp to the act of launching or retrieving that boat, preventing the ramp from being blocked for other purposes.
source_note: Parks & Wildlife Code Sec. 31.100(b) -- Interference With Markers or Ramps

question: Is it lawful in Texas to anchor a boat in the traveled portion of a river or channel if doing so blocks other boats from passing safely?
choice_a: Yes, a boater may anchor anywhere in a channel regardless of the effect on other traffic
choice_b: This restriction applies only to rivers, never to channels connecting lakes
choice_c: This restriction applies only to vessels longer than 26 feet
choice_d: No -- Texas law prohibits anchoring a boat in the traveled portion of a river or channel in a manner that prevents, impedes, or interferes with the safe passage of other boats through the area
explanation: Texas law prohibits anchoring in the traveled portion of a river or channel in a way that prevents, impedes, or interferes with safe passage of other boats, and separately prohibits anchoring near a state boat ramp in a way that blocks its use.
source_note: Parks & Wildlife Code Sec. 31.101 -- Obstructing Passage

question: May a boater legally operate a vessel inside a water area clearly marked by buoys or another distinguishing device as a bathing, fishing, or swimming restricted area?
choice_a: No, except for a patrol or rescue craft, or in the case of an emergency
choice_b: Yes, as long as the operator proceeds at headway speed through the marked area
choice_c: Yes, restricted-area markings in Texas are advisory only and carry no legal force
choice_d: No boater may ever enter such an area, even a patrol boat responding to an emergency
explanation: Texas law prohibits operating a boat within a clearly marked bathing, fishing, swimming, or otherwise restricted area, with an exception for patrol or rescue craft and for emergencies.
source_note: Parks & Wildlife Code Sec. 31.102 -- Operating Boats in Restricted Areas

question: How close may a vessel legally operate to a buoy or another vessel that is properly displaying a 'diver down' flag in Texas?
choice_a: There is no minimum distance as long as the operator keeps a careful watch
choice_b: No closer than 50 feet
choice_c: No closer than 5 feet
choice_d: No closer than 500 feet
explanation: Texas law prohibits operating a vessel within 50 feet of a buoy or vessel properly displaying a 'diver down' flag marking a scuba diving or snorkeling area.
source_note: Parks & Wildlife Code Sec. 31.1021(a) -- Operating Vessels in Scuba Diving or Snorkeling Areas

question: Within 150 feet of a properly displayed 'diver down' flag, at what speed must a vessel operate in Texas?
choice_a: Full cruising speed is permitted as long as the vessel stays at least 50 feet away
choice_b: The vessel must come to a complete stop and shut off its engine entirely
choice_c: No faster than the minimum speed necessary to maintain steerageway and headway
choice_d: There is no speed restriction once a vessel is more than 50 feet away
explanation: Texas law requires a vessel within 150 feet of a buoy or vessel displaying a 'diver down' flag to operate no faster than the minimum speed needed to maintain steerageway and headway.
source_note: Parks & Wildlife Code Sec. 31.1021(b) -- diver-down speed zone

question: What must a 'diver down' flag look like under Texas law to receive legal protection under the scuba/snorkeling operating rules?
choice_a: Any flag of any size or color, as long as it is flown from a pole on the shoreline
choice_b: A solid orange flag with no other markings
choice_c: A blue-and-white checkered flag identical to a racing flag
choice_d: A square or rectangular red flag at least 15 inches by 15 inches, bearing a diagonal white stripe
explanation: Texas law defines a 'diver down' flag as a square or rectangular red flag at least 15 inches by 15 inches with a diagonal white stripe; a diver or snorkeler must display this flag to receive the section's protections.
source_note: Parks & Wildlife Code Sec. 31.1021(f) -- diver-down flag definition

question: How close may a swimmer or diver legally approach a sight-seeing or excursion boat in Texas, absent an exception?
choice_a: No closer than 200 yards, except for maintenance purposes or within an enclosed area
choice_b: Texas law places no distance restriction on swimmers or divers near excursion boats
choice_c: No closer than 200 feet
choice_d: Swimmers and divers may never come within a mile of any excursion boat
explanation: Texas law prohibits a swimmer or diver from coming within 200 yards of a sight-seeing or excursion boat, except for maintenance purposes or within an enclosed area.
source_note: Parks & Wildlife Code Sec. 31.099(b) -- swimmer/diver distance from excursion boats

question: What penalty can a Texas boater face for a conviction of reckless operation under Parks & Wildlife Code Section 31.096?
choice_a: A verbal warning only, since reckless operation carries no possible fine or jail time
choice_b: A fine of not less than $200 nor more than $2,000, confinement in jail for up to 180 days, or both
choice_c: Automatic permanent forfeiture of the vessel, with no other possible penalty
choice_d: A flat $25 citation and nothing more, regardless of the circumstances
explanation: A conviction for reckless operation and excessive speed under Section 31.096 can carry a fine of not less than $200 nor more than $2,000, up to 180 days in jail, or both.
source_note: TPWD Operation of Your Boat / Parks & Wildlife Code Sec. 31.096 -- reckless operation penalty

question: What is the penalty range for a second BWI (Boating While Intoxicated) conviction in Texas?
choice_a: The identical penalty as a first offense, with no increase for a repeat conviction
choice_b: A mandatory 20-year prison sentence with no possibility of a shorter term
choice_c: A fine of up to $4,000 and confinement in jail of up to one year
choice_d: A fine of exactly $50 with no possibility of jail time
explanation: A second BWI conviction in Texas can carry a fine of up to $4,000 and up to one year of confinement, a substantial increase over the penalty for a first offense.
source_note: TPWD Operation of Your Boat -- BWI second-offense penalty

question: What is the penalty for a third BWI (Boating While Intoxicated) conviction in Texas?
choice_a: The same fine and jail term that applies to a first offense
choice_b: A fine only, with no possibility of imprisonment regardless of the number of prior convictions
choice_c: Automatic suspension of the vessel's registration, with no criminal penalty at all
choice_d: A fine of up to $10,000 and imprisonment of not less than 2 years nor more than 10 years
explanation: A third BWI conviction in Texas escalates to a fine of up to $10,000 and imprisonment of not less than 2 years nor more than 10 years.
source_note: TPWD Operation of Your Boat -- BWI third-offense penalty

question: Under Texas Penal Code Section 49.06, which classifies a first BWI conviction as a Class B misdemeanor, what minimum jail term applies?
choice_a: A minimum confinement term of 72 hours
choice_b: There is no minimum; a judge may impose zero jail time on any first conviction
choice_c: A minimum of 30 days
choice_d: A minimum of one full year
explanation: Texas Penal Code Section 49.06 classifies BWI as a Class B misdemeanor with a minimum term of confinement of 72 hours, distinct from the up-to-180-day maximum.
source_note: Texas Penal Code Sec. 49.06(b) -- BWI minimum confinement

question: Besides having an alcohol concentration of 0.08 or more, what is the other legal basis on which a person can be convicted of BWI under Texas Penal Code Section 49.01?
choice_a: Having consumed any measurable amount of alcohol at any point within the preceding 24 hours, regardless of any current effect
choice_b: Not having the normal use of mental or physical faculties by reason of the introduction of alcohol, a controlled substance, a drug, a dangerous drug, or a combination of those substances
choice_c: Having a prior DWI conviction, regardless of the person's current condition
choice_d: There is no alternative basis; a 0.08 blood alcohol concentration is the only way Texas law defines intoxication
explanation: Texas Penal Code Section 49.01 defines 'intoxicated' two ways: not having the normal use of mental or physical faculties due to alcohol or drugs, or having an alcohol concentration of 0.08 or more -- so a person can be convicted of BWI on the faculties standard even without a confirmed 0.08 reading.
source_note: Texas Penal Code Sec. 49.01(2) -- definition of 'intoxicated'

question: Can a person be charged with BWI in Texas while paddling a canoe or kayak, rather than operating a motorboat?
choice_a: No, BWI can only be charged against a person operating a vessel with a motor rated at 15 horsepower or more
choice_b: No, BWI applies exclusively to personal watercraft (PWCs)
choice_c: Yes -- Texas Penal Code defines 'watercraft' broadly to include a vessel, water skis, an aquaplane, or another device for transporting a person on water, other than a device propelled only by the current of the water, so BWI can apply to non-motorized craft like canoes and kayaks
choice_d: No, Texas law exempts all human-powered vessels from intoxication offenses entirely
explanation: The Penal Code's definition of 'watercraft' for intoxication offenses covers a vessel, water skis, an aquaplane, or similar device for transporting a person on water, excluding only devices moved solely by the current -- so a paddled canoe or kayak still qualifies, and BWI can be charged against its operator.
source_note: Texas Penal Code Sec. 49.01(4) -- definition of 'watercraft' for intoxication offenses

question: What offense, and at what severity, does Texas law impose on a person who operates a watercraft while intoxicated with a passenger younger than 15 years old aboard?
choice_a: The identical Class B misdemeanor as ordinary BWI, with no enhancement for the child's presence
choice_b: A civil traffic infraction only, with no criminal charge
choice_c: A Class C misdemeanor with a fine capped at $50
choice_d: Boating While Intoxicated with a Child Passenger, a state jail felony
explanation: Texas Penal Code Section 49.061 elevates BWI to a state jail felony -- Boating While Intoxicated with a Child Passenger -- when the intoxicated operator's watercraft carries a passenger younger than 15.
source_note: Texas Penal Code Sec. 49.061 -- Boating While Intoxicated with a Child Passenger

question: What offense applies in Texas when a person, by accident or mistake, causes serious bodily injury to another while operating a watercraft while intoxicated?
choice_a: Intoxication Assault, a felony of the third degree
choice_b: Simple BWI, with no additional or elevated charge regardless of the injury caused
choice_c: A Class C misdemeanor, the lowest possible offense level
choice_d: No additional criminal liability beyond the standard BWI offense
explanation: Texas Penal Code Section 49.07 creates the offense of Intoxication Assault, a third-degree felony, when a person intoxicated while operating a watercraft causes serious bodily injury to another by accident or mistake.
source_note: Texas Penal Code Sec. 49.07 -- Intoxication Assault

question: What offense and felony degree applies in Texas when a person, by accident or mistake, causes the death of another while operating a watercraft while intoxicated?
choice_a: Intoxication Manslaughter, treated only as a Class A misdemeanor
choice_b: Intoxication Manslaughter, a felony of the second degree
choice_c: No separate offense exists; the incident is prosecuted only as ordinary BWI
choice_d: A felony of the third degree, identical to Intoxication Assault
explanation: Texas Penal Code Section 49.08 makes Intoxication Manslaughter a second-degree felony when a person intoxicated while operating a watercraft causes another's death by accident or mistake.
source_note: Texas Penal Code Sec. 49.08 -- Intoxication Manslaughter

question: If a person arrested for BWI while operating a watercraft with an engine rated below 50 horsepower refuses to provide a breath or blood specimen, does Texas's Administrative License Revocation process automatically suspend that person's driver's license, the way refusal during a DWI vehicle stop would?
choice_a: Yes, refusal always triggers an automatic license suspension regardless of the watercraft's engine size
choice_b: Refusing a specimen has never carried any legal consequence in a Texas BWI investigation
choice_c: No -- for BWI arrests, there is no automatic driver's license suspension for refusing to provide a specimen unless the watercraft's engine is rated 50 horsepower or more
choice_d: Refusal automatically results in permanent confiscation of the boat instead of any license action
explanation: Under Texas's Administrative License Revocation guidance, there is no automatic driver's license suspension for refusing a breath or blood specimen in a BWI case unless the watercraft is powered by an engine rated 50 horsepower or more -- a notable departure from the vehicle DWI refusal rule.
source_note: Texas Water Safety Act -- ALR Process special note (administrative license revocation guidance)

question: What rule applies to a minor operating a watercraft in Texas who has any detectable amount of alcohol in their system, even below the 0.08 adult BAC threshold?
choice_a: Minors are held to the exact same 0.08 threshold as adults, with no lower standard for underage operators
choice_b: No violation occurs unless the minor's blood alcohol concentration reaches 0.08, identical to an adult
choice_c: Texas law does not address alcohol use by minors operating watercraft
choice_d: The minor may be cited and released for a Class C offense, with an automatic driver's license suspension, under Texas's zero-tolerance policy for minors and alcohol
explanation: Texas applies a zero-tolerance standard to minors operating watercraft: any detectable amount of alcohol can result in a Class C citation and an automatic driver's license suspension, well below the 0.08 threshold that applies to adults.
source_note: Texas Water Safety Act -- ALR Process special note, minor zero-tolerance provision

question: May a city, county, or other political subdivision of Texas charge a boater a fee to register or inspect a vessel used on public water within its jurisdiction?
choice_a: No -- Texas law prohibits a political subdivision from imposing or collecting a fee for the registration or inspection of vessels used on public water
choice_b: Yes, any city or county may set its own registration and inspection fees for vessels
choice_c: Only counties may charge such a fee; cities are barred from doing so
choice_d: Such fees are allowed only if TPWD approves them on a case-by-case basis
explanation: While a local government may designate restricted areas and adopt boat operation rules, Texas law specifically bars any political subdivision from imposing or collecting a fee to register or inspect a vessel used on public water.
source_note: Parks & Wildlife Code Sec. 31.092(e) -- local regulation fee prohibition

question: For a first-time violation of a vessel operation provision, what alternative to paying a fine may a Texas court allow a defendant to pursue?
choice_a: Texas courts have no authority to defer or waive a fine for a boating violation under any circumstance
choice_b: The court may defer imposition of the fine and place the defendant on probation for up to 60 days to complete an approved boater education course, waiving the fine upon successful completion
choice_c: The only alternative offered is unpaid litter-collection community service along the shoreline
choice_d: The defendant may pay half the fine in exchange for surrendering the vessel's title to the state
explanation: For a first-time violation of a vessel operation provision, a Texas court may defer the fine and place the defendant on up to 60 days of probation to complete an approved boater education course, waiving the fine if the course is completed successfully.
source_note: Parks & Wildlife Code Sec. 31.130 -- Boater Education Course Permitted in Lieu of Fine

question: Besides the 50-foot proximity rule and the nighttime ban, what does Texas law separately prohibit a PWC operator from doing?
choice_a: Wearing a life jacket while operating the PWC
choice_b: Operating the PWC during daylight hours under any circumstance
choice_c: Operating in a manner that requires the operator to swerve at the last possible moment to avoid a collision
choice_d: Carrying any passenger at all, even one wearing a life jacket
explanation: Texas law separately prohibits operating a personal watercraft in a manner that requires the operator to swerve at the last possible moment to avoid a collision, a distinct rule from the 50-foot proximity and nighttime restrictions.
source_note: Parks & Wildlife Code Sec. 31.106(a)(9) -- Personal Watercraft operating prohibitions

question: Does the PWC rule against operating within 50 feet of another vessel, person, platform, object, or shore (except at headway speed) apply on every Texas waterway without exception?
choice_a: Yes, the 50-foot rule applies identically on every body of water in Texas with no exceptions
choice_b: No, the rule applies only on waterways wider than 1,000 feet
choice_c: No, the rule applies only to PWCs longer than 12 feet
choice_d: No -- that 50-foot proximity rule does not prohibit operating a personal watercraft on bodies of water less than 100 feet in width
explanation: Texas law carves out an exception to the PWC 50-foot proximity rule for bodies of water that are less than 100 feet wide, since maintaining that distance would often be impossible on such narrow water.
source_note: Parks & Wildlife Code Sec. 31.106(c) -- Personal Watercraft 50-foot rule exception

question: Under Texas law, what is required of the operator of a motorboat under 26 feet in length that is equipped by the manufacturer with an engine cutoff switch (ECOS), while the boat is underway at greater than headway speed?
choice_a: The operator must first verify the switch is operational and properly attach the lanyard or wireless man-overboard transmitter to their body, clothing, or personal flotation device
choice_b: The engine cutoff switch is optional equipment that never needs to be worn or activated
choice_c: Only passengers, never the operator, are required to use the engine cutoff switch
choice_d: The requirement applies only to motorboats longer than 26 feet
explanation: Texas law requires the operator of a motorboat under 26 feet equipped with an engine cutoff switch to verify it is functional and to properly attach the lanyard or wireless transmitter before operating at greater than headway speed, so the engine shuts off automatically if the operator falls overboard.
source_note: Parks & Wildlife Code Sec. 31.1071 -- Operation of Motorboat With Emergency Engine Cutoff Switch
